statement: The Ifá priesthood (babaláwo) is historically male-dominated/male-exclusive in most documented lineages. Whether women can legitimately be initiated as Ifá priests (Ìyánífá, "Mother of Secrets") is a genuinely live, contested question — not a single unified "traditional" position. The controversy sharpened publicly at a 2006 global Ifá meeting in Venezuela, where Cuban babaláwos told a female Ifá initiate "there is no such thing as a woman Ifá priest," while Nigerian babaláwo present argued for women's acceptability. This is explicitly a Nigeria-vs-Cuban-lineage disagreement.
scholarly_disagreement: Whether female Ifá initiation (Ìyánífá) is legitimate — Cuban Lucumí and some Nigerian lineages reject it grounded in lineage tradition and specific Odù readings; other Nigerian lineages and the Ìyánífá/Ìyáláwo movement initiate women and treat this as legitimate/traditional.

sources.citation: "Mamalawo? The Controversy Over Women Practicing Ifa Divination." Utambuzi: Journal for the Study of the Religions of Africa and its Diaspora, University of Johannesburg journals platform.

interpretations.position: Female Ifá initiation is illegitimate; Ifá priesthood is reserved for men per lineage tradition and specific Odù readings around ritual restrictions tied to the Òrìṣà Odù

holders.name: Orthodox Cuban Lucumí lineages and some Nigerian lineages, per the 2006 Venezuela meeting account

interpretations.strongest_case: Grounded in specific, named lineage-transmitted readings of the Odù corpus.

interpretations.position: Female Ifá initiation (Ìyánífá) is legitimate and traditional

holders.name: Nigerian lineages participating in the Ìyánífá/Ìyáláwo movement, per the 2006 Venezuela meeting account

interpretations.strongest_case: Nigerian babaláwo present at the 2006 meeting argued directly for this position against the Cuban lineage rejection.
